newsitem.title: JAPAN: Finance firm joins Japan's growing insolvency list.
newsitem.headline: Finance firm joins Japan's growing insolvency list.

text.p: A Japanese loan company, Koei Corp, filed for court-protected liquidation on Monday with debts of more than 260 billion yen ($2 billion), the latest corporate casualty of "bubble" era loans gone bad.
The collapse, in debt terms, is the biggest so far this year in Japan.

Koei, an unlisted loan company involved in real estate-related lending, said it filed for managed liquidation at the Tokyo District Court on Monday with total debts of 264.1 billion yen ($2.16 billion).

This makes it the nation's biggest insolvency case this year and the ninth biggest case involving a non-bank financial institution in Japanese corporate history, leading credit research firm Teikoku Databank Ltd said.

Like other companies which have landed in the bankruptcy courts over the past few months, Koei buckled under the weight of debts resulting from aggressive lending during Japan's 1980s "bubble" of soaring asset prices and unbridled consumption.
It tried to restructure its business under a five-year plan but failed to turn things around, said Teikoku Databank, which specialises in insolvency data.
Japan's Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ), a leading commercial bank, holds a small stake in Koei, which is majority owned by its board members, as well as having loans outstanding to the company.
A Koei official said in late December that Koei's debts totalled 259.4 billion yen ($2.12 billion) at the end of March 1996, of which 61.2 billion yen ($501 million) was in loans from the IBJ.
The official also said at that time that Koei's other creditors included Sumitomo Trust & Banking Co Ltd, with outstanding loans of 9.6 billion yen ($78.6 million) to Koei.
Banking industry sources said despite the size of the collapse, the fallout from Koei's liquidation would be limited as the firm warned last year that it might have to be wound up.
"We were informed late last year that Koei would seek special liquidation so our loss from Koei's move was already covered by loan-loss provisions," one bank official said.
Non-bank financial institutions make loans but cannot take deposits, relying heavily on borrowed money from banks, which can therefore can be heavily exposed if the firms fold.

Other big bankruptcies so far this year include a sushi take-out chain, Kyotaru Co Ltd, which expanded aggressively in the bubble years, and Coco Yamaoka Hoshokuten, a jewellery retailer. ($1=122 yen)
